Currently, Sky's PSM holds approximately $2.7 billion in USDC within a single Ethereum address; if Circle were to blacklist that address at the request of law enforcement, the entire reserve could be frozen, potentially impairing redemptions and the peg stability of DAI and USDS. In response, the Sky Frontier Foundation stated that the flagged transactions do not mean all funds were stolen assets, noting that the volume accounts for less than 0.06% of PSM's over $930 billion in cumulative volume and occurred almost entirely via third-party DEX aggregators rather than Sky's official website, which implements wallet screening. — link

Neither application has been approved. DCM registration would allow Binance US to offer derivatives trading, including futures and options, while DCO registration would allow it to clear those trades. Binance US plans to use both registrations to offer U.S. users regulated derivatives, including perpetual futures. It has not launched any derivatives products and must await formal CFTC approval before doing so.

According to the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) website, BAM Derivatives LLC submitted Binance US’s application to register as a designated contract market (DCM). CFTC Chair: Onchain Platforms Like Hyperliquid Must Register or Partner With Licensed Exchanges to Enter US Market, Citing Backpack Model

CFTC Chair Michael Selig said onchain platforms such as Hyperliquid must register as exchanges or partner with registered exchanges to offer derivatives to U.S. retail users. They must follow the same rules as traditional exchanges but may still use onchain technology. He cited Backpack, which recently secured futures commission merchant (FCM), designated contract market (DCM) and derivatives clearing organization (DCO) approvals as a compliance basis for entering the U.S. market.

On prediction markets, Selig said the CFTC would work with the Justice Department to defend its federal authority over lawful derivatives contracts against state lawsuits. He also said a single-stock perpetual contract is not necessarily a security-based swap simply because it has no expiry date: its classification depends on its structure, and perpetual funding rates resemble the variation margin settlement used in traditional futures. — link
